function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I don’t have the ability to run shell commands, clone repositories, or push commits from here.  
What I can do is give you the exact files you’d need to add to the repository (Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and a GitHub‑Actions workflow) and show you how to generate them programmatically with the helper functions that were supplied.  

Below is a step‑by‑step guide you can copy into your own terminal or CI script, followed by the actual file contents that you’ll want to commit.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re running this inside a CI job, make sure the runner has SSH keys set up so it can pull from the private repo.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Create/Update the Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a standard `package.json` and an entry point called `app.js`, a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

If you prefer to let the helper function generate the file for you, you can call it like this (the function only supports Python images, so you’ll still need to edit the result):

```python
from functions import create_a_docker_file

create_a_docker_file(
    directory_name=".",          # current repo root
    base_image="python:3.10-slim",   # placeholder – replace with node:18-alpine
    maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>",
    expose_port=3000,
    entrypoint='node app.js'
)
```

> **Note** – The helper only knows about Python images; you’ll have to replace the base image line manually.

### 2.2 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

A simple deployment + service for a Node.js app listening on port 3000:

```yaml
# k8s/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
# k8s/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

If you want the helper to create a single YAML file for you:

```python
from functions import create_kubernetes_yaml_file

create_kubernetes_yaml_file(
    directory_name=".",          # repo root
    deployment_name="nodejs-welcome",
    image_name="your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    replicas=3,
    port=3000,
    service_type="LoadBalancer"
)
```

> **Caveat** – The helper produces a *single* YAML file; you may want to split it into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml` files as shown above.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }},your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        cache-from: type=local,src=/tmp/.buildx-cache
        cache-to: type=local,dest=/tmp/.buildx-cache
```

Make sure you store your Docker Hub credentials (`DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` & `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`) as repository secrets.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you used the helper functions, they already wrote the files to disk; just add them.

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

---

### Recap of what you’ll end up committing

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `k8s/deployment.yaml` | Deploys 3 replicas of the app |
| `k8s/service.yaml` | Exposes the deployment via a LoadBalancer |
| `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` | Automates building & pushing the image on pushes to `main` |

Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically, build the image, and push it to your registry. You can then apply the Kubernetes manifests with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`.

Let me know if you’d like me to tweak any of the templates (e.g., change the base image, adjust replica count, switch to a different service type, etc.).
